strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: reference-based motion customization for fast distilled text-to-video models, which existing training-free methods handle poorly due to coarse denoising and mismatched sampling behavior.

Proposes a novel training-free test-time distillation framework that uses a high-quality teacher model to guide a distilled student model through endpoint prediction, interpolation, and adaptive teacher supervision.
Introduces an adaptive acceleration strategy that dynamically schedules teacher guidance and truncates inner denoising steps, improving the practical quality-efficiency trade-off.

Provides extensive experiments across two distilled video generators (T2V-TurboV2 and AnimateDiff-Lightning), two benchmarks, multiple baselines, ablation studies, user study, and numerous qualitative examples in the supplementary material.
Demonstrates consistent improvements in motion fidelity, text alignment, and FID while remaining competitive with training-based and training-free baselines on inference time.
The method is clearly described, with a well-organized pipeline, equations, algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter details, and public code release statement.
Includes limitations, ethical/social impact discussion, and generator-level flexibility, which are valuable for the community.
weaknesses: Although the method is faster than many baselines, it still incurs substantial overhead relative to the base distilled model (e.g., 13s vs. 4s for T2V-TurboV2), so the claim of preserving high efficiency is relative rather than absolute; memory and dual-model inference costs are not analyzed.

The adaptive guidance strategy relies on heuristic thresholds and model-specific hyperparameters, with limited sensitivity analysis for key values such as δ1, δ2, W, Nmax, and τ; broader generalization of these settings is unclear.

Evaluation is limited to relatively small benchmark sets (e.g., 66 video-edit pairs and 15 videos), and motion fidelity metrics can be noisy or incomplete for complex, non-rigid motion; the user study covers only 36 samples with 50 participants.
The contribution is somewhat incremental, combining existing ideas—motion guidance, test-time distillation, and adaptive scheduling—without deep theoretical analysis or guarantees.
The ablation study is useful but incomplete in places (e.g., FID is not reported in the main ablation table), and failure cases are not systematically analyzed beyond brief qualitative examples.
The method depends on the availability of a suitable teacher model; performance when no strong teacher is accessible or when teacher-student domain gaps are larger remains underexplored.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practical problem: enabling training-free motion customization for fast distilled text-to-video models, where existing training-free methods often fail due to coarse denoising and mismatched sampling behavior.

Proposes MotionEcho, a well-motivated test-time distillation framework that uses a fine-grained motion-controllable teacher model to guide a distilled student during inference, avoiding additional model training.
Introduces an adaptive acceleration strategy with step-wise guidance activation and dynamic truncation, effectively balancing motion fidelity and inference efficiency.

Provides extensive empirical validation across multiple distilled video generators (e.g., T2V-TurboV2, AnimateDiff-Lightning) and benchmarks (TurboBench, AnimateBench), including quantitative comparisons, qualitative results, user study, and ablation studies.

The paper is clearly written and includes useful supplementary details such as pseudo-code, additional ablations, hyperparameter analysis, and discussion of limitations and ethical impacts. Reproducibility is supported by implementation details and a promise to release source code.
weaknesses: The method introduces several sensitive hyperparameters and thresholds (e.g., δ1, δ2, τ, λ, η, k, W, Nmax), and although ablations are provided, their robustness and transferability across datasets, motion types, and base models are not fully established.

The teacher-guided test-time distillation adds computational overhead, including potential backward passes through the teacher for score distillation. While the adaptive strategy reduces cost, a more thorough analysis of total compute, memory, and wall-clock time relative to training-free baselines would strengthen the efficiency claims.

The technical novelty is moderate: test-time distillation and motion guidance are existing concepts, and the contribution is primarily a well-engineered integration for distilled video generators rather than a fundamentally new algorithm or theoretical insight.

Some comparisons may not be perfectly apples-to-apples because baselines use different base models, training regimes, or motion customization strategies (e.g., VideoCrafter2 vs. T2V-TurboV2, training-based vs. training-free). Clarifying the fairness protocol and controlling for base model capacity would improve the empirical case.

The evaluation focuses on a limited set of benchmarks and motion categories; broader stress tests, failure cases, and more detailed discussion of when the method underperforms would help assess its practical reliability.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and under-explored problem: training-free motion customization for fast distilled video generators, where existing training-free methods often fail due to coarse denoising and mismatched sampling dynamics.

The proposed MotionEcho framework is technically plausible, combining teacher-guided test-time distillation with step-wise guidance activation, dynamic truncation, and endpoint prediction/interpolation.
Experiments are conducted on two distilled video models (T2V-TurboV2 and AnimateDiff-Lightning) and include quantitative comparisons, qualitative visualizations, ablation studies, and a user study.

The method shows improved motion fidelity and FID over several baselines in the reported tables, and the supplementary material provides an algorithm listing, additional qualitative results, and discussion of ethical impacts.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the method largely integrates existing components such as MotionClone/MotionDirector-style motion guidance, consistency distillation, teacher-student distillation, and heuristic adaptive scheduling. The core contribution is more of an engineering combination than a fundamentally new algorithm.

The comparisons are not well controlled. The proposed method uses an additional pre-trained teacher video diffusion model and performs teacher-side optimization at inference, whereas several baselines (e.g., MotionClone, DMT) do not receive the same auxiliary model or comparable compute budget. This undermines the fairness of the reported superiority and efficiency claims.

Efficiency claims are questionable. In Table 1, the proposed method takes 13s, while MotionClone is listed as 1s and T2V-TurboV2 16 steps as 4s in Table 3. The method is therefore not efficient relative to the distilled student model or the fastest training-free baseline, despite the paper claiming high efficiency.

The reported improvements are mixed and often marginal. Temporal consistency is slightly lower than MotionClone (0.976 vs. 0.978), text alignment gains are small, and the main improvements are in motion fidelity and FID. No confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or repeated-run variance are provided for the metrics or the user study.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Code is not released; several critical hyperparameters and scheduling choices (e.g., delta1, delta2, tau, Nmax, exact step-wise activation rules) are not fully specified; thresholds are selected by grid search without a clear validation protocol; and random seeds are not discussed.

The evaluation is limited to two teacher-student combinations. The paper does not thoroughly analyze sensitivity to teacher quality, domain gap between teacher and student, or generalization to a broader range of distilled video generators.

The writing is dense and notation-heavy in places, making some equations and algorithm steps hard to follow. Additional detail is needed for key components, such as exactly how teacher-side motion guidance is applied within each inner denoising step and how the adaptive schedule affects convergence or output stability.

strengths: Identifies and clearly articulates a significant limitation in applying existing training-free motion customization methods to distilled (few-step) video generators, attributing it to the sparse denoising steps and altered generative dynamics.
Proposes MotionEcho, a novel and technically sound test-time distillation framework that adaptively corrects the student model's sampling trajectory using a high-quality teacher model.

The mathematical formulation for the trajectory correction (Score Interpolation as an Echo) elegantly bypasses the intractable Jacobian computation by optimizing in the clean-data space, yielding a closed-form linear interpolation solution.

The adaptive acceleration strategy (step-wise guidance activation and dynamic truncation) effectively balances motion fidelity with computational efficiency, preventing excessive overhead from the teacher model.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation across multiple backbone architectures (UNet-based T2V-Turbo-V2, DiT-based Video-Blade, AnimateDiff-Lightning, Wan2.1/Wan2.2) and diverse benchmarks (TurboBench, DavisBench, AnimateBench, LOVEU-TGVE).
Demonstrates substantial improvements in motion fidelity and text alignment while maintaining fast inference speeds, outperforming both training-free and training-based baselines in efficiency.
The paper is well-structured, with clear explanations of the methodology, helpful visualizations (Figures 1, 2, 3), and detailed pseudo-code (Algorithm 1) in the appendix.
Good reproducibility practices, including detailed hyperparameters, implementation specifics, and an open-source commitment.
Thoughtful discussion of limitations (e.g., structural mismatch failure cases) and ethical/societal impacts in the appendix.
weaknesses: The method introduces some inference overhead in terms of peak GPU memory (PM), increasing from ~27 GB to ~36 GB on the TurboV2 backbone, which might strain standard consumer-grade hardware despite the acceptable inference time.

The framework assumes access to a suitable high-quality teacher model with a shared latent space and compatible architecture during inference, which is a notable constraint for arbitrary pre-trained distilled models.

Although the closed-form interpolation avoids the Jacobian, the reliance on a moving average of motion loss (with fixed window size W) for the adaptive acceleration strategy might be sub-optimal for highly irregular or rapidly changing motion dynamics.

While the paper demonstrates strong results on the tested models, the generalizability to other emerging distillation paradigms (e.g., adversarial distillation with entirely different trajectory properties) remains to be fully explored.

strengths: The paper identifies a critical and timely problem: existing training-free motion customization methods fail on distilled fast video generators due to altered denoising dynamics and the loss of dense intermediate states required for score guidance. The analysis of this failure mode is thorough and well-supported by preliminary experiments.

The proposed MotionEcho framework provides an elegant and technically sound solution to this problem. The use of a high-quality teacher model for selective test-time trajectory correction, combined with the clever score interpolation formulation (Eq. 5, Appendix C), avoids the intractable Jacobian computation and acts as a lightweight, effective gradient step in the clean-data space.

The adaptive acceleration strategy is well-designed, dynamically triggering teacher guidance based on moving average motion loss and truncating iterations early based on loss smoothness. This ensures that the efficiency advantages of distilled models are largely preserved while restoring motion fidelity.

The experimental validation is exceptionally comprehensive. The authors evaluate the method across multiple distilled backbones (UNet-based like TurboV2 and AnimateDiff-Lightning, DiT-based like Video-Blade, Wan2.1, Wan2.2, CogVideoX) against numerous baselines. The quantitative results (Tables 1-12), qualitative comparisons (Figures 1-25), and the user study (Figure 6) provide strong and consistent evidence for the method's superiority in motion fidelity, text alignment, and temporal consistency.

The paper is well-written, clear, and visually well-structured. The supplementary material is highly detailed, providing pseudo-code, extensive hyperparameter analyses, additional benchmarks (e.g., LOVUE-TGVE), and a thorough limitations section alongside societal impact considerations.

The mathematical derivation of the proposed score interpolation as a proximal form is clear and contributes to the paper's technical depth, making the method theoretically grounded and easy to implement.
weaknesses: The method incurs additional inference overhead compared to pure distilled generation (e.g., ITC increases from 7s to 13s on TurboV2) due to occasional teacher invocations. While the adaptive strategy minimizes this, it still requires a high-quality teacher model to be loaded in memory, adding a computational burden (e.g., peak memory increases from 27GB to 36GB on TurboV2).

A minor failure case is presented in Appendix D (transferring a human climbing motion to a monkey). This highlights a general limitation of latent-space motion guidance when significant structural discrepancies exist between the source subject and the target generation, which is an inherent challenge in this paradigm.

The closed-form interpolation step (Eq. 5) relies on a single gradient update in the clean-data space. While computationally efficient, a deeper analysis or ablation comparing this against a more expensive multi-step optimization in the clean space (if feasible) could further strengthen the justification for the chosen approximation.

strengths: Clearly identifies and analyzes the failure of existing training-free motion customization methods on distilled text-to-video models, including qualitative and empirical evidence of motion degradation.

Proposes MotionEcho, a novel training-free test-time distillation framework that uses teacher-guided trajectory correction via endpoint prediction and interpolation, with an adaptive acceleration strategy to schedule teacher supervision.

Conducts extensive experiments across multiple distilled backbones (TurboV2, Video-Blade, TDM, Wan2.2 variants) and benchmarks, with ablations, user study, computational analysis, and supplementary results.
Provides detailed method derivation, pseudo-code, hyperparameter settings, and reproducibility details; discusses limitations and ethical/social impacts.
weaknesses: The main quantitative tables compare baselines largely on full teacher models rather than applying all competing training-free methods to the same distilled student models; fairer comparisons on distilled backbones are mostly relegated to the appendix, which weakens the central claim about failure of existing methods on distilled models.

Although training-free, the method adds test-time teacher guidance and optimization overhead (e.g., TurboV2 inference increases from 7s to 13s), and it assumes access to a suitable paired full teacher model, partially reducing the claimed efficiency and generality.
The adaptive scheduling strategy depends on several hyperparameters that appear tuned per backbone or motion type, and robustness/sensitivity to these choices is not fully explored in the main paper.

Some benchmark sizes and the user study are relatively small, and comparisons omit certain recent training-free baselines when directly applied to distilled models, which may limit the strength of the empirical conclusions.
